question.text: Mr. Arjun Menon, founder of Shakti Special Situations Cat III AIF, pitches a contrarian strategy that buys deeply beaten-down stocks after sharp negative news (overreaction). Behavioural finance literature attributes such opportunities to which underlying driver and what is the AIF-manager implication?

answer.text: Strong-form efficiency; no implication for AIF managers.

Investor behavioural biases (overreaction to bad news, loss aversion, representativeness) produce temporary mispricings; a disciplined contrarian AIF can exploit reversals, provided it survives the drawdown window and respects risk limits.
Random walk with positive drift; the AIF can safely ignore risk.
SEBI mandates contrarian investing for Cat III AIFs.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 3.3 and broader behavioural-finance context, overreaction / underreaction anomalies reflect investor biases (De Bondt-Thaler type). A contrarian AIF can harvest these reversals but must survive the mark-to-market drawdown - i.e., have matched LP capital lock-ups, risk limits and liquidity buffers. The Trap: Option A denies the alpha source. Option C ignores risk. Option D invents a SEBI mandate that does not exist. Cross-Exam Context: XV (RA), XXI-B (PM), X-B (IA L2) test behavioural biases. XIX-C emphasis: match your strategy's drawdown profile to the fund's lock-up and LP liquidity tolerance - a mismatch triggers forced selling at the worst time. Manager's Pro-Tip: For contrarian/deep-value Cat III strategies, negotiate longer LP lock-ups or gated redemption in the PPM - otherwise LP redemption pressure during the drawdown phase will force you to sell exactly what you should be buying.
